title: Alakena
author: Laker Grace
desc: Termites collected during their emergence, cleaned and ground to a paste-like consistency, with groundnuts or vegetables if you want them — and the winged ones dried and kept for later.
longDesc: Alakena is the Lango termite dish, made from Macrotermes species — ngwen generally, and okok for the soldier termites. It is the northern counterpart to the Ganda nswaa, and the treatment is different: rather than roasting them as a snack, the termites are cleaned and ground into a paste. It is also the best-cited of the thinly documented Ugandan dishes, with real nutritional figures behind it, and those figures are why it is worth taking seriously as food rather than as curiosity.
equipment: Grinding stone, or a mortar and pestle
steps: Collect the termites during their emergence.
Grind them into a paste-like consistency.
Add groundnuts or vegetables if you want them.
Dry the winged termites and store them for later.
chefTips: Collect during the emergence. Termites come out of the ground in swarms after rain, and that window is the only time you get them.
Ground to a paste, not roasted whole. That is what makes this alakena rather than a termite snack, and it is the northern treatment.
Dried winged termites keep, which is how a household eats them out of season.
Groundnuts and vegetables are optional additions, and groundnut is the obvious one — it turns the paste into a sauce.
Two named types go in: ngwen is the general term and okok the soldier termites.

The nutritional figures are worth knowing because they are unusually well documented for a dish like this: lysine at 1.0 to 1.3 milligrams per gram, iron at 70.7 to 111.8 milligrams per hundred grams, and zinc at 4.4 to 16.2. Those iron figures are extraordinary.
No quantities are documented in any source. This is the honest shape of the record and nothing has been estimated.
The Ganda pounded-termite treatment in UGA062 — cleaned, roasted, sun-dried, pounded to flour and prepared as luwombo — is the closest documented parallel and is worth reading alongside this.
commonMistakes: Trying to buy them out of season.
Roasting them whole and calling it alakena.
Grinding them so coarse the paste never forms.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Alakena, which describes it as a termite-based dish of the Lango people using Macrotermes species termites locally called ngwen and soldier termites called okok, with optional groundnuts and vegetables, prepared by collecting the termites during their emergence, cleaning them and grinding them into a paste-like consistency, with dried winged termites preserved for later consumption.

Its nutritional figures — lysine 1.0 to 1.3 mg/g, iron 70.7 to 111.8 mg/100 g, zinc 4.4 to 16.2 mg/100 g — are carried here. That article has eight citations and they are academic: Busitema University, Brill journals, Scientific Reports, the Journal of Food Composition and Analysis, the Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine, ResearchGate and Oxford Academic. It carries no maintenance banner.
No quantities are documented. None has been estimated.
The Ganda pounded-termite treatment, which is the closest documented parallel, is from the Slow Food Uganda booklet p43 and appears in this collection as UGA062.
storage: Dried termites keep for months. The paste, 2 days refrigerated.
healthBenefits: Documented iron at 70.7 to 111.8 mg per 100 g, which is exceptional for any food.
Documented zinc at 4.4 to 16.2 mg per 100 g and lysine at 1.0 to 1.3 mg/g.
High in protein and in fat, with almost no carbohydrate.
Wild-harvested, seasonal, and with no farming input at all.
culturalNote: Two communities, the same insect, two completely different dishes — the Baganda pound termites into flour for luwombo, the Lango grind them into a paste called alakena. That is the kind of divergence that only becomes visible when you record the local names rather than writing up a country's food as one cuisine.
